passage:
Monday. Ujjwal, five, watered the class plants and shared his crayons. Parveen ma'am said, "Good job, Ujjwal!" three times.
Tuesday. He spilled paint on Mehul's drawing, and Parveen ma'am said sharply, "Ujjwal, look where you're going!" He stood very still, lip wobbling.
Friday. At home, Papa asked, "How was school this week?" Ujjwal hugged his knees. "Parveen ma'am shouted at me." He didn't mention the plants, or the crayons, or the three "good jobs". Papa asked, "Anything nice?" Ujjwal thought hard, then shrugged.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday?
qa.a: He spilled paint on Mehul's drawing.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal only talk about being shouted at?
qa.a: The sharp moment hurt and stuck with him, so it felt bigger than the three 'good jobs' from Monday.

qa.q: How could Papa help Ujjwal remember the good parts of his week?
qa.a: Papa could gently ask about the class plants or sharing crayons, and tell him that one spill doesn't undo all the good things he did.

qa.q: How might Parveen ma'am feel if she heard Ujjwal's version of the week?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little sad that one sharp moment counted more for him than her praise, and might soften her tone next time.

grounding: It shows a young boy remembering one scolding far more than several moments of praise.

passage:
The power had gone out in the Kolkata flat, and Arnab, four, couldn't sleep in the heat. His mother Gopika fanned him with a newspaper. "What was the best part of today?"
Arnab's lip trembled. "Dadu said I was naughty."
He had pulled the cat's tail once, in the morning. After that he'd sung for Dadu, fed the fish and eaten all his rice, and Dadu had clapped each time.
"Dadu also clapped when you sang," Gopika said softly.
"But he said naughty." Arnab turned his face to the wall.
Gopika kept fanning, and began to hum his song.

qa.q: What did Arnab do after pulling the cat's tail?
qa.a: He sang for Dadu, fed the fish and ate all his rice.

qa.q: Why does 'naughty' matter more to Arnab than all the clapping?
qa.a: The one scolding hurt, so it feels heavier and stays in his mind, pushing out the happy moments.

qa.q: What else could Gopika try to help Arnab?
qa.a: She could name each good moment with him slowly, like the song and the fish, or ask Dadu to remind him tomorrow how much he enjoyed the singing. 🙂

qa.q: How might Dadu feel if he knew Arnab went to bed upset?
qa.a: Dadu might feel sorry that one word stuck, when he clapped far more than he scolded.

grounding: It shows a small boy on a hot, dark night holding on to one scolding more than many moments of praise.

passage:
At Tenzin's school in Bengaluru, Nirmala miss put stickers on the chart every day. Tenzin, six, had five gold stars for reading and one frowning face from the day he pushed in the lunch line.
At pick-up his uncle said, "Show me your chart!"
Tenzin pointed straight at the frowning face. "That's me. I was bad."
"And these?" His uncle tapped the stars.
"Those are just stars." Tenzin kicked a pebble. "Nirmala miss was cross."
His uncle crouched down. "Five stars and one frown. Which is more?" Tenzin counted on his fingers, frowning.

qa.q: How many gold stars did Tenzin have?
qa.a: Five gold stars for reading.

qa.q: What does Tenzin pointing straight at the frowning face suggest?
qa.a: That the one telling-off hurt and felt like the truth about him, so it outweighed the five stars he'd earned.

qa.q: What is good about the uncle's question?
qa.a: Asking him to count stars and frowns lets Tenzin see for himself that the good outnumbers the bad, without being told to cheer up.

qa.q: How might Nirmala miss feel if she saw Tenzin calling himself bad?
qa.a: She might be surprised that one frowning face mattered more than the stars, and want to tell him he's a good reader who made one mistake.

grounding: It shows a young boy fixing on one frowning sticker over five gold stars.

passage:
"Ma, Mamu shouted at me."
"When, Arnab?"
"At the wedding. I touched the flowers on the car."
Gopika looked at him in the rear-view mirror. "And what about when you danced? Everyone clapped. Nani said you were the best dancer."
"Mamu shouted."
"And the aunty who gave you two laddoos for helping carry the plates?"
Arnab pulled his knees up. "He said DON'T in a big voice."
"Mamu said sorry after, remember? He lifted you up."
"But he shouted first." Arnab looked out of the window, his lip wobbling.

qa.q: What did Arnab touch at the wedding?
qa.a: He touched the flowers on the car.

qa.q: Why does Arnab keep coming back to Mamu shouting?
qa.a: The one loud "DON'T" hurt and scared him, so it feels much bigger than the clapping, the laddoos and even Mamu's sorry 🥺

qa.q: What could Gopika try next to help Arnab with the hurt?
qa.a: She could first say that the shout felt scary, and then, once he feels heard, remind him of the dancing and the clapping.

qa.q: How might Mamu feel if he heard that the shout was all Arnab remembered?
qa.a: Mamu might feel sorry and surprised, since he apologised and lifted Arnab up, and never meant one sharp word to spoil the day.

grounding: It shows a young child remembering one scolding more strongly than many moments of praise at a family wedding.

passage:
Dance teacher's note, Saturday kids' class (Harsha)
Uday, 5, had a lovely class. I praised him five times: his jumps, helping a new girl, the clap pattern, waiting his turn, his big smile.
Once he pushed past another child, and I said firmly, "Uday, no pushing."
At pick-up he told his father, "Harsha teacher doesn't like me. She said no pushing." Nothing else.
I knelt and told him I liked his jumps and his helping, and that "no pushing" was about the pushing, not about him. He still looked unsure.
Next: repeat the praise at the start of next class; keep reminders short.

qa.q: How many times did Harsha praise Uday?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he said Harsha teacher doesn't like him?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unsure, because the one firm "no pushing" felt heavier than all five bits of praise.

qa.q: Which step by Harsha could help Uday most, and why?
qa.a: Kneeling down to separate the pushing from Uday himself, and planning to repeat the praise next class, helps the good moments stick as firmly as the one telling-off.

qa.q: How might Uday's father see the class after hearing "Harsha teacher doesn't like me"?
qa.a: His father might worry at first that Uday had a bad day, until he learns from Harsha about the five kind comments.

grounding: It shows a young child remembering one firm correction far more strongly than several moments of praise.

passage: At the kindergarten in Porto, Ivan had been praised all week: for sharing blocks, for tidying up, for helping Camila with her shoes. On Friday he knocked over the blue paint, and Miss Rosa said sharply, "Ivan! Look what you did!" That weekend, when his dad asked about school, Ivan said only, "Miss Rosa was cross." On Monday he walked past the easel with his hands behind his back and wouldn't touch the brushes. Camila held one out to him. He shook his head hard.

qa.q: What did Ivan knock over on Friday?
qa.a: He knocked over the blue paint.

qa.q: Why did Ivan keep his hands behind his back at the easel?
qa.a: Ivan still felt hurt and afraid of being told off again; the one sharp moment felt bigger than a whole week of praise.

qa.q: What could Miss Rosa do to help Ivan paint again?
qa.a: Miss Rosa could invite him back to the easel warmly, remind him of the good things he did all week, and show that spills can simply be cleaned up.

qa.q: How might Camila see Ivan refusing the brush?
qa.a: Camila, whom Ivan helped with her shoes, may be puzzled or a little sad that her friend won't paint.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering a single scolding more strongly than a week of praise.

passage: At the playschool gate, Joseph's mother asked how the day had been. "Indu Miss shouted at me," he said, lip out. Indu Miss, overhearing, knelt down. That morning she had told him "well done" for counting to ten, clapped when he fed the fish and hugged him when he shared his biscuit. Then, just once, at lunch, she had said loudly, "Joseph, no throwing rice!" "Remember the fish?" she asked gently. Joseph shrugged. He only remembered the rice.

qa.q: What did Indu Miss clap for?
qa.a: She clapped when he fed the fish.

qa.q: Why did Joseph tell his mother only about the shouting?
qa.a: Joseph felt hurt by the loud 'no throwing rice', and that one sore moment felt heavier than all the well-dones, the clapping and the hug.

qa.q: How could Indu Miss or Joseph's mother help him hold on to the good parts?
qa.a: They could talk through the whole day with him at the gate, naming the counting, the fish and the biscuit alongside the rice.

qa.q: What might Indu Miss feel when Joseph says she shouted at him?
qa.a: Indu Miss might feel a pang of sadness that the praise didn't stick, and want to remind him gently of the good moments.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering the one time he was told off more than many moments of praise.

passage:
Tuesday. At swimming class, the coach gave Asif three stars on the chart: for kicking, for floating, and for being brave with his face in the water. Then Asif splashed a big girl, and the coach blew the whistle hard. "No splashing, Asif!"
Thursday. Asif hid under the bed when it was time to go. "Coach hates me," he whispered to his big sister Bhavna.
Saturday. Bhavna took him to see the chart at the pool. She pointed at his stars. "One, two, three." Asif touched each one, then climbed into the water.

qa.q: How many stars did Asif get on the chart?
qa.a: He got three stars on the chart.

qa.q: Why did Asif whisper 'Coach hates me' on Thursday?
qa.a: Asif felt hurt and scared after the hard whistle, and that one telling-off felt bigger than the three stars.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She showed him his stars on the chart and counted them, so the good moments felt as real to him as the whistle.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have felt when Asif hid under the bed?
qa.a: Bhavna was probably worried for her little brother and wanted to show him the coach had praised him too.

grounding: Shows a young child letting one sharp telling-off outweigh several pieces of praise, until he is shown the praise again.

passage: It was the last day of the Onam holidays, and rain was hammering the tin roof. Madhav had helped Amma make the flower carpet all morning. "Beautiful! Clever boy!" she said. Then he knocked over the water pot, and she said sharply, "Madhav, careful!" At bedtime, his older cousin Nitin asked, "How was your day?" Madhav's lip wobbled. "Amma shouted at me." "What else?" "Just the shouting." Nitin laughed. "She said 'clever boy' about ten times. I counted." Madhav thought. "She did?" "And the flowers?" Madhav looked at the carpet. "I made the yellow part," he whispered.

qa.q: What did Madhav knock over?
qa.a: The water pot.

qa.q: Why did Madhav only remember the shouting at bedtime?
qa.a: The one sharp word hurt so much that he felt sad and small, and it pushed out all the praise from the morning.

qa.q: How did Nitin help Madhav remember the good parts?
qa.a: He told Madhav that Amma said "clever boy" about ten times and pointed him to the flower carpet he made.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she knew Madhav only remembered the shouting?
qa.a: Amma might feel sad and surprised, since she had praised him many times and only spoken sharply once.

grounding: Shows a young child during Onam remembering one sharp word more strongly than many words of praise.

passage: One cold winter morning in Lucknow, Vijay's playschool made paper lanterns for the Christmas fair. Miss praised Vijay three times: for his bright colours, for sharing glue, for helping Pranav fold his lantern. Then Vijay tore the paper by mistake, and Miss said, "Oh, Vijay, gently!" At home, his mother asked about school. "Miss was angry with me," Vijay said, hiding his face in her shawl. "Anything else?" "No." Pranav's mother laughed. "Pranav said Miss told Vijay he was the best helper." Vijay peeked out. "She did?" He showed his mother his lantern.

qa.q: How many times did Miss praise Vijay?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he hid his face in his mother's shawl?
qa.a: He felt sad and ashamed, as if Miss had only been angry, because the one sharp word stuck more than the praise.

qa.q: How did Pranav's mother's news help Vijay?
qa.a: It reminded him that Miss called him the best helper, so he remembered the good parts of his day.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel about telling his mother Vijay was the best helper?
qa.a: Pranav probably felt happy for his friend and proud to share good news.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering one sharp word from his teacher more than three bits of praise during a winter craft day.

passage:
"Minakshi didi, Papa scolded me today."
"Why, Mohit?"
"I spilled the rangoli colours on the step. Red everywhere."
"Oh no. What else happened today?"
"Nothing."
"Nothing? It's Diwali. Didn't you light diyas?"
"Yes."
"And what did Papa say about your diyas?"
"...He said I did them very neatly."
"And the sweets you gave Dadi?"
"She said I was her good boy."
"So how many good things, and how many scoldings?"
"Lots of good. One scolding."
"Which one are you thinking about?"
"The scolding."
"Shall we think about the diyas now?"
"Okay. The diyas were nice."

qa.q: What did Mohit spill on the step?
qa.a: The rangoli colours. Red everywhere.

qa.q: Why was Mohit only thinking about the scolding?
qa.a: The one scolding made him feel sad and hurt, and it felt heavier than all the praise, so it filled his mind.

qa.q: How did Minakshi didi help Mohit?
qa.a: She asked about each good part of his day, the diyas and the sweets, until he could see there were many good things and only one scolding.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he knew Mohit remembered only the scolding?
qa.a: Papa might feel sorry, since he praised Mohit's diyas too.

grounding: Shows a young child at Diwali remembering one scolding more strongly than the many times he was praised.

passage:
Nursery note, Christmas week. Written by Zeenat, class teacher.
This week Francis was praised many times: for sharing crayons, for singing loudly at carol practice, for tidying the blocks. He smiled each time and moved on.
On Wednesday I told him firmly to stop running near the Christmas tree. His chin wobbled.
Today, when I asked what he liked about school this week, he said, "You said no at the tree." Nothing about carols or crayons.
What I did next: I told him the tree rule was about safety, not about him being bad. Then we drew three stars, one for each good thing, and stuck them on his cubby.

qa.q: What was Francis told to stop doing?
qa.a: Francis was told firmly to stop running near the Christmas tree.

qa.q: Why did Francis remember the scolding more than the praise?
qa.a: The scolding felt big and sad to Francis, so it stuck, while the smiles for crayons and carols passed quickly.

qa.q: Why was drawing three stars a good next step?
qa.a: The stars made the good moments visible, so Francis could hold them as firmly as the one scolding.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel hearing Francis's answer?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel surprised and a little sad that one firm rule outweighed so much praise.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering one firm scolding more strongly than many moments of praise.

passage:
During the sugarcane harvest, Kunal helped Reena Aunty every day. He carried the small basket. He fed the calf. Everyone said, "Shabash, Kunal!"
One evening he tipped over the milk pot. Reena Aunty said sharply, "Kunal! Look where you walk!"
That night, Kunal wouldn't eat. "Reena Aunty is angry with me," he whispered to his mother.
"She said shabash so many times today," his mother said.
Kunal shook his head. He only remembered the milk.
Next morning Reena Aunty handed him the small basket again. "My best helper," she said, and gave him a piece of sugarcane.

qa.q: What did Kunal tip over?
qa.a: Kunal tipped over the milk pot.

qa.q: Why wouldn't Kunal eat that night?
qa.a: Kunal felt sad and worried that Reena Aunty was angry, because the one sharp word felt bigger than all the shabash.

qa.q: What did Reena Aunty do the next morning that helped?
qa.a: Reena Aunty gave Kunal the small basket, called him her best helper and gave him sugarcane, showing the scolding didn't erase the praise.

qa.q: How does Kunal's mother see the day?
qa.a: Kunal's mother sees a day full of praise and reminds him that Reena Aunty said shabash many times.

grounding: Shows a young child during the harvest who remembers one sharp scolding more than many words of praise.

passage:
It was the first snowy week at the kindergarten in Bergen. Jin built a snow tunnel, and Ingrid, his teacher, clapped. He shared his red spade. "Kind, Jin!" He zipped his own jacket. "Clever!"
Then he threw a snowball at a girl's face. "Jin, no. Faces are not for snow," Ingrid said, firm.
At pickup, his father asked, "How was today?"
Jin stared at his boots. "Bad. Ingrid said no."
"Only no?"
"Only no."
Ingrid heard and crouched down. "Jin, I also said kind, and clever, and great tunnel. Remember?"
Jin looked up slowly, as if checking whether that was allowed.

qa.q: What did Jin build in the snow?
qa.a: Jin built a snow tunnel.

qa.q: Why did Jin say the day was bad?
qa.a: Jin felt sad and ashamed, because the one firm 'no' stuck more than being called kind and clever.

qa.q: What did Ingrid do at pickup, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ingrid crouched down and reminded Jin of the praise too, helping him weigh the good moments against the one no.

qa.q: How might Jin's father feel hearing 'only no'?
qa.a: Jin's father may feel concerned and puzzled, hearing a whole day summed up by one word.

grounding: Shows a young child who remembers one firm 'no' more strongly than several moments of praise.

passage: At the Christmas party in the playschool, Joseph sir gave Kamal a gold star sticker for singing. That week he had also praised Kamal's drawing, his tidy shoes and his sharing. But on Tuesday sir had said, "Kamal, no running!" in a loud voice. When Mumma came to pick him up, she asked about the party. Kamal pulled at his sticker. "Sir shouted at me," he said, lip trembling. "He doesn't like me." "Didn't he give you this star?" Mumma asked. Kamal looked at the star as if he had forgotten it was there.

qa.q: What did Joseph sir give Kamal at the Christmas party?
qa.a: A gold star sticker for singing.

qa.q: Why does Kamal think Joseph sir doesn't like him?
qa.a: The one loud "no running" felt so hurtful that it stuck and pushed out all the praise, so Kamal feels sad and unsure.

qa.q: How could Mumma help Kamal remember the whole week?
qa.a: She could go through the good moments with him, like the star, the drawing and the tidy shoes, and explain that sir said "no running" to keep him safe.

qa.q: How might Joseph sir feel if he knew what Kamal remembered?
qa.a: Joseph sir might feel surprised and a bit sorry, since he praised Kamal many times and only meant to stop him running.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering one scolding more strongly than many moments of praise.
